facts.statement: Lagerpeton was first described by Alfred S. Romer in 1971 from fossils found in the Chañares Formation of Argentina.
facts.quote: First described from the Chañares Formation of Argentina by A. S. Romer in 1971

facts.statement: The name Lagerpeton combines the Greek words for 'hare' and 'reptile'.
facts.quote: The name comes from the Greek λαγώς (, "hare") plus ἑρπετόν (, "reptile").

facts.statement: All known Lagerpeton fossils have been found exclusively in the Chañares Formation of La Rioja Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: Lagerpeton fossils have only been collected from the Chañares Formation in La Rioja Province, Argentina.

facts.statement: A smaller specimen, MCZ 4121, was described by Romer in 1972 and was preserved in a nodule alongside fossils of Lewisuchus and Lagosuchus.
facts.quote: In 1972, Romer described MCZ 4121, which was a specimen smaller than the holotype.

facts.statement: Andrea Arcucci described two additional specimens, PVL 4619 and PVL 4625, in 1986.
facts.quote: Andrea Arcucci described two PVL specimens, PVL 4619 and 4625, in 1986.

facts.statement: Lagerpeton is estimated to have been about 70 cm (28 inches) long based on hindlimb measurements.
facts.quote: Lagerpeton is estimated to have been 70 cm (28 in) in length based on the length of the hindlimb

facts.statement: Scientists have identified twenty-one unique anatomical characters specific to L. chanarensis.
facts.quote: Twenty one autapomorphic characters have been identified in L. chanarensis

facts.statement: Lagerpeton lacks key dinosaurian features like the anterior trochanter, placing it at the base of Dinosauromorpha or potentially outside the group entirely.
facts.quote: L. chanarensis lacks many dinosaurian characters, such as the anterior trochanter, placing it basal within Dinosauromorpha or even outside the group altogether.

facts.statement: The oldest Lagerpeton fossils date to the Upper Middle Triassic (Ladinian) period and were found in Gondwana, part of southern Pangaea.
facts.quote: The oldest fossils of L. chanarensis were found in the Chañares Formation and originate from the Upper Middle Triassic (Ladinian) of Gondwana, southern Pangaea.

facts.statement: Radiometric dating places the Chañares Formation and its fossils between 236 and 234 million years old.
facts.quote: Radiometric dating of volcanic material in the formation has narrowed the formation and entire fossil assemblage found there to between 236 and 234 million years old.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that modern small bipedal mammals that leap (saltators) are the closest living analogues to Lagerpeton.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that the extant analogues most similar to L. chanarensis are small bipedal mammals, which are often saltators.

facts.statement: Lagerpeton possesses anteriorly inclined neural spines on its dorsal vertebrae, a feature common in leaping mammals but unique among archosaurs.
facts.quote: The neural spines of the posterior dorsal vertebrae are inclined anteriorly, a character not observed in any other archosaur, but common in saltatory mammals.

facts.statement: The pelvic girdle of Lagerpeton is remarkably small relative to its hindlimb length.
facts.quote: Relative to the hindlimb length, the pelvic girdle is remarkably small.

facts.statement: Lagerpeton had a narrow foot with only two functional toes, a trait similar to modern leaping mammals.
facts.quote: The narrow and functionally didactyl pes are a further similarity to modern saltators.

facts.statement: The hypothesis that Lagerpeton was a leaping animal is currently debated among scientists.
facts.quote: The hypothesis of saltatorial locomotion is debated, however.

facts.statement: Some researchers argue that the small pelvic girdle and reduced toes could instead indicate a running (cursorial) lifestyle rather than leaping.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the size of the pelvic girdle and lateral digital reduction may be equally used as evidence for cursorial locomotion.

facts.statement: Footprints from Poland dating to the Early to Late Olenekian show a quadrupedal dinosauromorph similar to Lagerpeton.
facts.quote: Early to late Olenekian trackways from Poland have yielded footprints of a Lagerpeton-like quadrupedal dinosauromorph.

facts.statement: If the Polish footprints belong to a close relative of Lagerpeton, the group's origins could be pushed back to the Early Triassic.
facts.quote: If this ichnogenus represents a close relative of Lagerpeton, it would push back the origin of this taxon to the Early Triassic

facts.statement: The existence of a quadrupedal basal dinosauromorph like Lagerpeton challenges the theory that bipedalism was the ancestral state for dinosaurs.
facts.quote: as a quadrupedal basal dinosauromorph, it also raises questions debating the theory that bipedalism is ancestral to dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Lagerpeton was about 0.7 meters long and had a unique foot with an unusually elongated fourth toe.
facts.quote: Medía cerca de 0.7 metros de largo y poseía un pie único, con un dedo cuarto inusualmente alargado.

facts.statement: Lagerpeton is related to Dromomeron, which lived during the Late Triassic in the southwestern United States.
facts.quote: Estaba relacionado con Dromomeron, que vivió durante el Triásico Superior en el suroeste de Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: All known fossils of Lagerpeton come exclusively from the Chañares Formation in La Rioja, Argentina.
facts.quote: Los fósiles conocidos de Lagerpeton proceden exclusivamente de la Formación Chañares, de la provincia de La Rioja, Argentina.

facts.statement: Alfred Romer described the species Lagerpeton chanarensis in 1971 based on a complete right hind limb.
facts.quote: En 1971, Alfred Romer describió la especie Lagerpeton chanarensis a partir de una extremidad posterior derecha completa

facts.statement: Andrea Arcucci described two PVL specimens, PVL 4619 and PVL 4625, in 1986.
facts.quote: En 1986, Andrea Arcucci describió dos especímenes del PVL: PVL 4619 y PVL 4625.

facts.statement: Lagerpeton is estimated to have reached an approximate length of 70 cm, calculated from its hind limb length.
facts.quote: Se estima que Lagerpeton alcanzaba una longitud aproximada de 70 cm, calculada a partir de la longitud de sus miembros posteriores.

facts.statement: Its body mass is estimated at less than 4 kg, based on the reduced cross-section of its limb bones.
facts.quote: Su masa corporal se ha estimado en menos de 4 kg, basándose en la reducida sección transversal de los huesos de las extremidades

facts.statement: Twenty-one autapomorphic characters have been identified in L. chanarensis.
facts.quote: En L. chanarensis se han identificado 21 caracteres autapomórficos

facts.statement: L. chanarensis lacks several dinosaur-specific characters, such as the anterior trochanter.
facts.quote: L. chanarensis carece de varios caracteres propios de los dinosaurios, como el trocánter anterior

facts.statement: Its lack of certain dinosaur traits supports its position as a basal dinosauromorph or even outside Dinosauromorpha, according to some hypotheses.
facts.quote: lo que sustenta su posición como un dinosauromorfo basal o incluso fuera de Dinosauromorpha, según algunas hipótesis.

facts.statement: The parent group of Lagerpeton is Lagerpetidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Lagerpetidae

facts.statement: Lagerpeton is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Lagerpeton lived during the Ladinian stage, between 241.464 and 237 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ladinian to Ladinian (241.464 to 237 million years ago)

facts.statement: Artistic reconstructions depict the animal in a dynamic running posture supported by its notably long and thin single hind leg.
facts.quote: El animal está capturado en una postura dinámica de carrera, apoyado sobre su única pata trasera notablemente larga y delgada.

rejected.quote: Alfred Romer named Lagerpeton chanarensis in 1971, based on a complete right hindlimb discovered during the MCZ-MLP expedition.

rejected.statement: The body mass of Lagerpeton is estimated to be no more than 4 kg based on the slender cross-section of its limb bones.
rejected.quote: Body mass has been estimated as no more than 4 kg, based on the slender cross section of limb bones
